prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms opened the 10^-18 regime of frequency measurement and made laboratory tests of gravitational redshift and fundamental constants possible

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as a single prize part, and the second round has made my reasons sharper rather than different. The new content is the magic-wavelength lattice: it cancels the light shift of the trapping field on the clock transition, so that thousands of neutral atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime and interrogated together. That gives stability and accuracy at the same time, which neither the frequency comb (a ruler for optical frequencies) nor ion control (single quantum systems, limited by signal-to-noise) could provide. The proof is experimental and reproduced: several independently built clocks at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST, PTB and SYRTE agree at the 10^-18 level, and a systematic error in one machine would not survive that comparison. The same machines resolve gravitational redshift over millimetres and set limits on varying constants and dark-matter couplings, so it is a clue from nature obtained by better measurement, not only a better instrument. Katori for the proposal and the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye for taking systematics and stability to the limit and for many-body clock physics, is the cleanest credit on the shortlist. Having read all eight statements, I do not see a competing configuration that is both as mature and as fairly creditable, and I see no reason to add a second part just to fill space.
statement.case_against: The honest weaknesses are three. First, lineage: the 2005 and 2012 prizes sit next to this one, Ye shared the 2005 prize, and a sceptic can read lattice clocks as the next increment in a clock series and as technique more than a new phenomenon. Mehlig and Eriksson are right that this is a question of judgement, not something the citation can dissolve by wording alone. Second, the credit is two people, and Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko and the Sr and Yb community, and the theorists of the light-shift cancellation, are outside it; the priority of the magic-wavelength idea relative to parallel proposals I can recall only from memory and have not verified from the papers. Third, the second has not been redefined and the thorium and ion clocks remain competitors, so some will say the committee should wait. I do not think waiting is warranted on the physics, but I cannot claim the outcome of that metrological decision.

responses.point: Mehlig accepts B002 as the best-credited candidate on the list but calls clean attribution a criterion of safety rather than of discovery, and finds a mechanism-level result such as KPZ more compelling than ever better accuracy.
responses.response: I accept the distinction and I do not rest the case on attribution. The question is whether lattice clocks recognise a mechanism or only a number. I think the answer is a mechanism: the magic-wavelength condition is a statement about differential light shifts of the two clock states that one engineers away, and it is what makes the many-atom regime exist at all. The number 10^-18 follows from it, and the redshift over a millimetre and the constraints on constants then show that this regime tells us something about nature. On KPZ, my first-round question stands and the chair has recorded it: I want to know what in the experimental confirmation is independent of the 1986 theory and reproduced beyond one liquid-crystal system. You also state that Parisi and the exact-solution authors lie outside the three names. For me that is the decisive obstacle for B056 as a complete part, because the most rigorous content would be left uncredited.

responses.point: Lindroth keeps B002 first, notes that cross-comparison between laboratories is the decisive evidence, and says the citation should not lean on the redefinition of the second; she also left priority of the magic-wavelength proposal unchecked.
responses.response: I agree with all three points and I have changed my draft citation accordingly: it no longer mentions the redefinition of the second at all, and it rests on magic-wavelength trapping, the 10^-18 regime and the redshift and constants tests. On the priority question the chair asked us two to report on. From memory, and I flag it as memory, Katori's group published the magic-wavelength proposal with Ido and Kuwata-Gonokami in 2003 and the first strontium lattice spectroscopy and clock demonstrations from 2003 to 2005, while Ye's group and Lemonde's group in Paris reached the Sr lattice clock in 2005 to 2006 with independent work on the light-shift cancellation. Nothing I recall displaces Katori as the originator of the scheme, but we should not write 'first' into the citation without the secretariat checking the papers. That also answers Eva Olsson: a 'for the invention and realisation' wording credits Katori's proposal and Ye's realisation to extreme accuracy without ranking one above the other.

responses.point: Olsson applies the test that the prize goes to the original experiment and not to a later, more spectacular realisation, and asks whether Katori's first demonstration or Ye's records are the right object of credit.
responses.response: I think the test is the right one and it gives a two-person answer here. Katori's group proposed the scheme and made the first demonstration, so he is the original. Ye's group did not merely do it better: they made the clock accurate enough and stable enough that the systematics, the cross-lab comparison and the many-body and redshift measurements became meaningful, which is what turned the proposal into a result about nature. Without his work the demonstration would remain a proof of principle; without Katori's the records would lack their origin. This is different from the case of a second group repeating a known result. I take your disclosure about the University of Tokyo seriously and note that I have no tie that cuts the other way, but it is the kind of institutional link the committee should record without treating it as disqualifying.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B015, a verified new state of matter, over a precision-measurement capability, and asks the committee to be explicit about whether a capability or a phenomenon is what it recognises, deferring to Lindroth and me on whether the 10^-18 tests amount to a discovery of nature.
responses.response: You asked me directly, so my answer is that it is both, and the order matters. A new capability recognised by this committee has always been a prize for what it makes observable: the lattice clocks give us a laboratory test of the gravitational redshift over a millimetre, bounds on drifts of constants and on ultralight dark matter that no other apparatus provides. I agree that B015 is a confirmed phenomenon and that the physics is robust. The difficulty I see is not its merit but the credit set: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe proposal that Molenkamp tested, and Zhang's death and the 3D contributors make a trio contestable, as you say yourself. With B002 the only open credit question is whether to name other people, not whether the two named are the right ones. For that reason I keep B015 outside my alternatives, though I would not oppose it as a second part if the committee found a defensible credit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will judge optical lattice clocks as a distinct achievement from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; this is a judgement and I have not found a sentence that removes the doubt for everyone.
Priority of the magic-wavelength proposal and of the first lattice clocks: my chronology is from memory and should be checked against the original papers before a citation is fixed.
Whether the 10^-18 agreement and the redshift and constants tests are enough for a citation if the second is not redefined within the next few years.

Which fallback is better if B002 is judged too close to earlier prizes, Cirac, Zoller and Blatt (B033) or Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger (B060); Zoller's appearance in both and the overlap with the 2012 prize make each of them imperfect.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict that requires recusal. Updated disclosure: I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory at JILA during my PhD, and Jun Ye works in that environment, so I have a loose scientific acquaintance with the community but no collaboration with Katori or Ye that I can identify from my profile. My Lund and WACQT affiliations bear mainly on B017 and quantum-information candidates (B033, B060 as alternatives), and I would flag that if either became decisive.
